newsitem.title: USA: U.S. air quality to be topic of public hearings.
newsitem.headline: U.S. air quality to be topic of public hearings.

text.p: Public hearings in four U.S. cities this week will be battlegrounds between industry groups and health advocates as the Clinton administration gathers views on its proposal to fight soot and smog pollution.

Hearings are set for Tuesday and Wednesday in Boston, Chicago and in Salt Lake City, Utah, on the proposal health advocates say will prolong and improve thousands of lives, but industry groups say will cost billions of dollars for minimal health benefits.
A hearing on technical issues is set for Tuesday in Durham, N.C.

Saying current standards do not adequately protect public health, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in late November proposed tightening allowable limits on smog-forming ozone pollution and airborne particles such as dust and soot. For the first time it called for a separate standard for the smallest particles that penetrate deep into lungs.

With the potential to affect virtually all smokestack industries and automobile use and to impose heavy costs on communities to clean up their air, the issue was expected to be one the most heavily lobbied of the year.

"Our goal is to highlight the crucial issue of children's health. There are a lot of asthmatic children whose lives would be different with these standards," Kathryn Hohmann, director of the Sierra Club's environmental programs, said.

"It gives us an opportunity to lay out to the EPA our case for why we think the scientific basis for changing these standards is so weak. And we'll also try to get them to understand that there are economic consequences to changing these standards that they haven't looked at carefully enough," Paul Bailey, of the American Petroleum Institute, said.

The EPA is slated to announce a final rule in June, but Congress likely will review it under a law passed last year that set up a formal process for Congress to weigh in on new regulations. That process could drag well into the fall.
This EPA proposal just would set air quality standards, not regulations on how to achieve those standards.

But industry groups led by the National Association of Manufacturers contend it would result in restrictions that would clamp down on industrial growth and job growth, and change Americans' way of life, including how often they can drive or fire up their outdoor barbeques.
They say those costs should be evaluated now, not after the goals are set and policymakers, industries and communities must figure out ways to meet them.

But health advocates say standards should be set to protect public health, including children, the elderly and chronically ill. Costs of reaching the standards should be considered later when policymakers work out measures and a schedule for meeting the goals, they say.
They also say industries fail to recognize the billions of dollars in benefits, including reduced hospital admissions and missed work-days, cleaner air would bring.
The EPA estimated costs of reaching standards at $6.5 billion to $8.5 billion a year, and benefits at $120 billion annually. Implementing new rules would be several years off.
This week's public hearings were scheduled concurrently to save time and prevent the same people from repeating arguments at several forums, an EPA official said.
The agency also will accept written comments and telephoned comments until the public comment period ends Feb. 18, and several congressional committees plan to hold hearings on the issues.
But this week's public hearings will be the first high-profile events, and both sides are planning a major lobbying effort next week.
Health and environmental groups plan to enlist churches, parents groups, senior citizens groups, doctors and health officials.

They also will sponsor radio spots in the four cities, and in Providence, R.I., home state of Senate Environment Committee Chairman John Chafee, a pro-environment Republican who has expressed concerns about potential costs of the rule.

Industry spokesmen said they planned to get support from medical experts, as well as state and local government officials concerned that the stricter rule would push their areas out of compliance with air standards and prompt more controls on industries, automobiles and development.
